nodes.summary: If a link-cut tree state $s$ is valid, then for every vertex $x$ the state obtained from $s$ by accessing $x$ is again valid.
nodes.title: Access preserves validity

nodes.summary: For every link-cut tree state $s$ and every vertex $x$, accessing $x$ changes only the preferred edges: the represented forest of the resulting state equals the represented forest of $s$.
nodes.title: Access leaves the represented forest unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ be a vertex of its represented forest. Then, after accessing $x$, the preferred-path decomposition of the new state contains a path $p$ whose last vertex is $x$, and $p$ is the path from the root down to $x$ in some tree of the represented forest of $s$.
nodes.title: After access, the accessed vertex ends its preferred path

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex. If $x$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$, let $T$ be the first such tree and let $p$ be the path in $T$ from its root down to $x$. Accessing $x$ keeps the represented forest and replaces the preferred edges by those preferred edges of $s$ whose parent endpoint is not on $p$, followed by the edges of $p$, each directed from parent to child.…
nodes.title: Access in a link-cut tree

nodes.summary: For every rooted tree $t$ and all vertices $a$ and $b$, if $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in $t$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t$.
nodes.title: Parent-child edges are edges

nodes.summary: For vertices $a$, $b$ and a rooted tree $t$ with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the adjacency test of $a$ and $b$ in $t$ returns true exactly when $r = a$ and some $c_i$ has root $b$, or $r = b$ and some $c_i$ has root $a$, or the adjacency test of $a$ and $b$ returns true in some $c_i$.
nodes.title: Adjacency test

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of its represented forest. If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$, and neither $a = x$ and $b = y$ nor $a = y$ and $b = x$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest obtained from $s$ by cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: An edge cut keeps every other edge

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $u$ be rooted trees and $y$ a vertex, and suppose that grafting $u$ as a new child under $y$ in $t$ succeeds and yields the tree $t'$. Then for all vertices $a$ and $b$, the vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$ if and only if they are adjacent in $t$, or adjacent in $u$, or $a = y$ and $b$ is the root of $u$, or $a$ is the root of $u$ and $b = y$.
nodes.title: Edges after grafting

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree with no repeated vertex and $x$ a vertex, and suppose that removing every subtree rooted at $x$ from $t$ leaves the tree $t'$ (that is, the root of $t$ is not $x$). If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t$ and both are vertices of $t'$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$.
nodes.title: Pruning keeps surviving edges

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree with no repeated vertex, and suppose that rerooting $t$ at a vertex $x$ yields the tree $t'$. Then for all vertices $a$ and $b$, the vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$ if and only if they are adjacent in $t$.
nodes.title: Rerooting keeps every edge

nodes.summary: Two vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a rooted tree $t$ when they are joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in either direction: some node of $t$ labelled $a$ has a child labelled $b$, or some node of $t$ labelled $b$ has a child labelled $a$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in a rooted tree

nodes.summary: For a link-cut tree state $s$ and vertices $x$ and $y$, $x$ and $y$ are connected in $s$ if and only if some tree of the represented forest of $s$ contains both $x$ and $y$ in its Euler tour.
nodes.title: Connectivity via Euler tours

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be vertices of its represented forest. Then in the state obtained from $s$ by linking $x$ to $y$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ are connected, that is, some represented tree contains both. No invariant on the state is needed.
nodes.title: Linking connects the endpoints

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be connected in $s$. Then $x$ and $y$ are still connected in the state obtained from $s$ by making $x$ the root of its represented tree.
nodes.title: Making a vertex the root keeps its connections

nodes.summary: Two vertices $x$ and $y$ are connected in a link-cut tree state $s$ when some tree of the represented forest of $s$ has both $x$ and $y$ among its vertices.
nodes.title: Connectivity in a link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: If $s$ is a valid link-cut tree state, then for every vertex $x$ the state obtained from $s$ by cutting off the subtree rooted at $x$ is again valid.
nodes.title: Cutting preserves validity

nodes.summary: If $s$ is a valid link-cut tree state, then for all vertices $x$ and $y$ the state obtained from $s$ by cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ is again valid.
nodes.title: Edge cutting preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$. Then cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ in $s$ gives the same state as first making $x$ the root of its represented tree and then cutting off the subtree rooted at $y$.
nodes.title: Edge cut on an adjacent pair

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in no tree of the represented forest of $s$. Then cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ in $s$ leaves the represented forest unchanged and makes the list of preferred edges empty.
nodes.title: Edge cut on a non-adjacent pair

nodes.summary: For vertices $x$ and $y$ and a link-cut tree state $s$, cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ works as follows. If $x$ and $y$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$, the result is obtained from $s$ by first making $x$ the root of its represented tree and then cutting off the subtree rooted at $y$. Otherwise the represented forest is left unchanged. In both cases the list of preferred edges…
nodes.title: Cutting an edge of a link-cut tree

nodes.summary: Cutting at a vertex $x$ resets the preferred edges of the state to the empty list and changes its forest as follows. If no tree of the forest contains $x$, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise let $T$ be the first tree containing $x$ and $S$ the first subtree of $T$ rooted at $x$ in preorder. Every tree containing $x$ is removed from the forest, and two trees are appended at the end: first the remainder of $T$ with…
nodes.title: Cutting off the subtree at a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a tree whose vertex list is duplicate-free, let $x$ be a vertex of $T$ with root path $p$ (the path from the root of $T$ down to $x$), and let $E$ be a list of directed edges such that every consecutive pair of $p$, parent first, lies in $E$, and every edge of $E$ whose first vertex lies on $p$ is such a consecutive pair. Then the downward preferred path of the preferred-path decomposition of $T$ under…
nodes.title: Access edges make the root path the downward preferred path

nodes.summary: For every list of preferred edges, the downward preferred path in the preferred-path decomposition of a tree is nonempty and its first vertex is the root of the tree.
nodes.title: The downward preferred path starts at the root

nodes.summary: For every list of preferred edges, in the preferred-path decomposition of a tree $T$, the downward preferred path and every other path are paths of $T$: any two consecutive vertices are joined by a parent-child edge of $T$, in either direction.
nodes.title: Decomposition paths are paths of the tree

nodes.summary: For every list of preferred edges, the downward preferred path of a tree followed by the concatenation of the other paths of its preferred-path decomposition is a permutation of the vertex list of the tree.
nodes.title: Preferred paths permute the vertex list

nodes.summary: Given a list $E$ of preferred edges, each a pair (parent, preferred child), the decomposition of a tree $T$ is a pair (down, rest): down is the preferred path that starts at the root of $T$ and follows edges of $E$ downward, and rest is the list of all other preferred paths of $T$. When a node has several children joined to it by edges of $E$ (excluded in valid states, where each vertex has at most one preferred…
nodes.title: Preferred-path decomposition of a tree

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a tree $T$, the subtree of $T$ rooted at the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder, or nothing when $x$ does not occur in $T$.
nodes.title: Subtree rooted at a vertex

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a forest given as a list of trees, the first tree whose vertices contain $x$, or nothing when no tree contains $x$.
nodes.title: Tree of a forest containing a vertex

nodes.summary: If $p$ is the path from the root of a tree $T$ down to a vertex $x$ of $T$, then $p$ is nonempty and its last (deepest) vertex is $x$.
nodes.title: A root path ends at its target

nodes.summary: For a vertex $y$ and trees $N$ and $T$, grafting $N$ at $y$ in $T$ attaches $N$ as a new last child of the first node of $T$ labelled $y$ in preorder, keeping every existing node and edge; it returns nothing when $y$ does not occur in $T$. This is the tree surgery behind linking two trees: it adds exactly the edge from $y$ to the root of $N$.
nodes.title: Grafting a tree below a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path of $x$ in $t$ (the path from the root of $t$ down to $x$) is defined and equals $p$, then $p$ is nonempty and its first vertex is the root of $t$.
nodes.title: The root path starts at the root

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path of $x$ in $t$ is defined and equals $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$, then for every $i < k$ the vertices $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ are adjacent in $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in one direction or the other.
nodes.title: Consecutive vertices of a root path are adjacent

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state. For every path $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$ in the preferred-path decomposition of $s$ and every $i < k$, some represented tree of $s$ has $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ adjacent, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in one direction or the other.
nodes.title: Preferred paths of a link-cut tree state follow represented edges

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $E$ any list of pairs of vertices, read as preferred (parent, child) edges. For every path $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$ in the preferred-path decomposition of $t$ under $E$ and every $i < k$, the vertices $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ are adjacent in $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in one direction or the other.
nodes.title: Preferred paths of a tree follow tree edges

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path of $x$ in $t$ is defined and equals $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$, then for every $i < k$ the vertex $p_i$ is the parent of $p_{i+1}$ somewhere in $t$.
nodes.title: A root path follows parent-child edges downward

nodes.summary: For every valid link-cut tree state $s$ and all vertices $x$ and $y$, the state obtained from $s$ by linking $x$ and $y$ is valid.
nodes.title: Linking in a link-cut tree preserves validity

nodes.summary: Given vertices $x$ and $y$ and a state $s$, the state $\operatorname{link}(x, y, s)$ has no preferred edges (all edges dashed), and its forest is defined as follows. If $x$ or $y$ is not a vertex of the forest, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise let $t_x$ and $t_y$ be the first represented trees containing $x$ and $y$. If $x$ is a vertex of $t_y$, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise $t_x$ is rerooted at $x$ (the…
nodes.title: Linking two trees of a link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: For every valid link-cut tree state $s$ and every vertex $x$, the state obtained from $s$ by making $x$ the root of its represented tree is valid.
nodes.title: Rerooting a link-cut tree state preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex of its represented forest. After making $x$ the root, some represented tree has root $x$ and contains $x$ as a vertex.
nodes.title: Making a vertex the root installs a tree rooted there

nodes.summary: Given a vertex $x$ and a state $s$, the state $\operatorname{makeRoot}(x, s)$ has no preferred edges (all edges dashed), and its forest is defined as follows. If $x$ is not a vertex of the forest, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise the first represented tree containing $x$ is rerooted at $x$: the edges on the path from its old root to $x$ are reversed, and when the tree has distinct vertices every undirected edge…
nodes.title: Making a vertex the root in a link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, let $x$ and $y$ be vertices, and let $t$ be the first tree of the represented forest of $s$ that contains $x$. Suppose no vertex occurs twice in $t$, and let $T_x$ be the subtree of $t$ rooted at $x$. If $y$ is a vertex of $t$ but not of $T_x$, then after cutting $s$ at $x$ both $x$ and $y$ are vertices of the represented forest.
nodes.title: Both sides of a cut remain in the forest

nodes.summary: If $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in a tree $t$, then $a$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: The parent endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex

nodes.summary: If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a tree $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in either direction, then $a$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: The first endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex

nodes.summary: For every link-cut tree state $s$ and every vertex $v$, $v$ lies on some path of the preferred-path decomposition of $s$ if and only if $v$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$. No validity hypothesis on $s$ is needed.
nodes.title: Preferred paths cover exactly the vertices of the forest

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex, let $t$ be the first tree of the represented forest of $s$ that contains $x$, and let $p$ be the path in $t$ from the root down to the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder. Then every edge of $p$, taken as the pair (parent, child) of consecutive vertices of $p$, is a preferred edge of the state obtained from $s$ by accessing $x$.
nodes.title: Access makes the root path preferred

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, $x$ a vertex, and $(u, w)$ a preferred edge of $s$, directed from the parent $u$ to the child $w$. Suppose that, if some tree of the represented forest of $s$ contains $x$, then $u$ does not lie on the path in the first such tree from its root down to the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder. Then $(u, w)$ is still a preferred edge after accessing $x$.
nodes.title: Access keeps off-path preferred edges

nodes.summary: If $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in a tree $t$, then $b$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: The child endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex

nodes.summary: If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a tree $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in either direction, then $b$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: The second endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex

nodes.summary: If $p$ is the path in a tree $t$ from the root down to a vertex $x$, then every vertex of $p$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: Root paths stay inside the tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $C$ be trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $C$ at $y$ in $t$, that is, attaching $C$ as a new last child of a node labelled $y$, produces the tree $t'$, then for every $v$, $v$ is a vertex of $t'$ if and only if $v$ is a vertex of $t$ or a vertex of $C$.
nodes.title: Vertices after grafting

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree whose preorder vertex list has no repeated vertex, and let $x$ be a vertex. Suppose the subtree search finds the subtree $s$ of $t$ rooted at $x$, and pruning $t$ at $x$ leaves the tree $t'$. Then every vertex of $t$ that is not a vertex of $s$ is a vertex of $t'$.
nodes.title: Pruning keeps the vertices outside the detached subtree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree and $x$ a vertex. If pruning $t$ at $x$ leaves the tree $t'$, then every vertex of $t'$ is a vertex of $t$ and is different from $x$.
nodes.title: Vertices of a pruned tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree and $x$ a vertex. If rerooting $t$ at $x$ yields the tree $t'$, then a vertex lies in $t'$ if and only if it lies in $t$.
nodes.title: Rerooting preserves the vertex set

nodes.summary: A vertex $x$ belongs to a link-cut tree state $s$ when $x$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$.
nodes.title: Vertex of a link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: Every preferred path of a valid state has distinct vertices.
nodes.title: Preferred paths have distinct vertices

nodes.summary: In a valid link-cut tree state, the concatenation of all preferred paths of the decomposition has no repeated vertex: no vertex occurs twice on one path or on two different paths.
nodes.title: Preferred paths cover each vertex at most once

nodes.summary: If the preorder vertex list of a rooted tree $t$ has no repeated vertex and $p$ is the path from the root of $t$ down to a vertex $x$, then $p$ has no repeated vertex.
nodes.title: Root paths have distinct vertices

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$. After the edge cut of $x$ and $y$ in $s$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ are not connected: no represented tree contains both.
nodes.title: Cutting an edge separates its endpoints

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, let $t$ be the first tree of its represented forest containing the vertex $x$, and let $u$ be the first subtree of $t$ in preorder whose root is $x$. After cutting $s$ at $x$, the vertex $x$ is not connected to any vertex $y$ that is not a vertex of $u$.
nodes.title: A cut disconnects a vertex from everything outside its subtree

nodes.summary: The forest built from the empty list is empty; the forest built from a list $r, c_1, \dots, c_k$ consists of the single spine $r \to c_1 \to \cdots \to c_k$, the rooted tree in which each vertex has the next one as its only child.
nodes.title: Forest from a vertex list

nodes.summary: In a valid link-cut tree state, any two preferred paths at different positions of the preferred-path decomposition have no vertex in common.
nodes.title: Preferred paths are pairwise vertex-disjoint

nodes.summary: For vertices $a$ and $b$ and a rooted ordered tree $t$, $a$ is a parent of $b$ in $t$ when some node of $t$ labelled $a$ has a child subtree whose root is $b$. Preferred edges of a link-cut tree are directed this way, from a node to its preferred child.
nodes.title: Parent-child relation in a rooted tree

nodes.summary: For a list of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n$, its path edges are the ordered pairs $(v_0, v_1), (v_1, v_2), \dots, (v_{n-1}, v_n)$ of consecutive vertices, in this order; a list with at most one vertex has no path edges. For a path listed from the root downward each pair is (parent, child), and the preferred edges installed by an access to a vertex $x$ are the path edges of the root-to-$x$ path.
nodes.title: Consecutive edges of a vertex path

nodes.summary: For a link-cut tree state $s$, its preferred paths are obtained by taking, for each represented tree of $s$ in forest order, the preferred paths of that tree under the preferred edges of $s$, and concatenating these lists. Within a tree these are its maximal chains of preferred edges when each vertex has at most one preferred child, each listed from its shallowest to its deepest vertex; a vertex incident to no…
nodes.title: Preferred-path decomposition of a link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be a forest of rooted ordered trees whose concatenated vertex lists have no duplicates, let $x$ be a vertex, and let $t$ be the first tree of $f$ containing $x$. Then the concatenated vertex list of the forest obtained from $f$ by removing every tree containing $x$, followed by the vertex list of $t$, is a permutation of the concatenated vertex list of $f$.
nodes.title: Removing the tree containing a vertex splits the forest's vertices

nodes.summary: For every list $E$ of directed edges and every rooted ordered tree $t$, the concatenation of the preferred paths of $t$ under $E$ is a permutation of the preorder vertex list of $t$.
nodes.title: The preferred paths of a tree rearrange its vertex list

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $s$ be rooted ordered trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $s$ as a new child at $y$ in $t$ succeeds and yields the tree $t'$, then the vertex list of $t'$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t$ followed by the vertex list of $s$.
nodes.title: Grafting adds the new subtree's vertices

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree whose vertex list has no duplicates and let $x$ be a vertex. If $x$ occurs in $t$, with $s$ the subtree of $t$ rooted at $x$, and pruning at $x$ leaves a tree $t'$ (that is, $x$ is not the root of $t$), then the vertex list of $t$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t'$ followed by the vertex list of $s$.
nodes.title: Pruning a subtree splits the vertex list

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex. If rerooting $t$ at $x$ yields the tree $t'$, then the vertex list of $t'$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t$.
nodes.title: Rerooting preserves the vertices

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex that does not occur in $t$. Then pruning the subtrees rooted at $x$ from $t$ succeeds and returns $t$ itself.
nodes.title: Pruning at an absent vertex changes nothing

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$, pruning $T$ at $x$ removes every subtree of $T$ whose root is labelled $x$, keeping every other node and edge and the order of children. If the root of $T$ is $x$, nothing remains and pruning is undefined. Otherwise the result is the tree with the same root whose children are, in their original order, the pruned children of the root, with the children labelled $x$…
nodes.title: Pruning the subtrees rooted at a vertex

nodes.summary: Given a vertex $x$ and a forest, given as a list of rooted ordered trees, removing the trees containing $x$ deletes from the list every tree that has $x$ among its vertices and keeps the remaining trees in their original order.
nodes.title: Removing the trees that contain a vertex

nodes.summary: For every rooted ordered tree $T$ and every vertex $x$ that is not a vertex of $T$, rerooting $T$ at $x$ is undefined (it returns no tree).
nodes.title: Rerooting fails at an absent vertex

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$ with root $r$, rerooting $T$ at $x$ is defined recursively. If $r = x$, the result is $T$ itself. Otherwise let $C$ be the first child subtree of $r$ that contains $x$, let $p$ be the root of $C$, and let $C'$ be $C$ rerooted at $x$. The result is $C'$ with the tree formed by $r$ and its remaining children (in their original order) attached as a new last child of the…
nodes.title: Rerooting a tree at a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $T$ and $N$ be rooted ordered trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $N$ into $T$ at $y$ is defined and yields the tree $T'$, then the root of $T'$ equals the root of $T$.
nodes.title: Grafting keeps the root

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$, the root path of $x$ is defined exactly when $x$ is a vertex of $T$. It is then the list of vertices on the path from the root of $T$ down to $x$, root first and ending with $x$; if $x$ occurs more than once, the path leads to its first occurrence in preorder.
nodes.title: Root-to-vertex path

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex. If pruning $T$ at $x$ yields a tree $T'$ (that is, the root of $T$ is not $x$), then the root of $T'$ equals the root of $T$.
nodes.title: Pruning keeps the root

nodes.summary: For a vertex $r$ and a list of vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the spine is the rooted tree $r \to c_1 \to \cdots \to c_k$: its root is $r$, each vertex has the next one in the list as its only child, and the last vertex ($c_k$, or $r$ when $k = 0$) is a leaf.
nodes.title: Path tree on a vertex list

nodes.summary: A state of a link-cut tree over a vertex type $V$ consists of the represented forest, a list of rooted ordered trees with vertices in $V$, and a list of preferred (solid) edges, each a pair $(u, v)$ of vertices meant as the edge from a node $u$ to its preferred child $v$ in the represented forest; the structure itself does not require these pairs to be edges of the forest. The preferred-path decomposition is…
nodes.title: Link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: For every rooted ordered tree $T$ and vertices $a$ and $b$, if $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $T$ (joined by a parent-child edge in either direction), then $b$ and $a$ are adjacent in $T$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in a tree is symmetric

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and let $E$ be a list of preferred edges, each a pair (parent, child). The preferred paths of $t$ under $E$ are listed as follows: first the downward path of the preferred-path decomposition of $t$ under $E$, which starts at the root of $t$ and follows preferred edges downward, and then all other paths of that decomposition, in the order the decomposition returns them.
nodes.title: Preferred paths of a tree

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state whose list of preferred edges is empty. If the concatenation of the vertex lists of the trees of the represented forest of $s$ has no duplicates, then $s$ is valid.
nodes.title: Validity of states with no preferred edges

nodes.summary: A link-cut tree state $s$ is valid when four conditions hold: the concatenation of the vertex lists of the trees of its represented forest has no duplicates (so the trees are vertex-disjoint); its list of preferred edges has no duplicates; every preferred edge $(a, b)$ is a parent-child edge of some tree of the represented forest, with $a$ the parent of $b$; and any two preferred edges with the same parent are…
nodes.title: Valid link-cut tree states
Computer Science

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
